title: Container With Most Water: opposite-end, move shorter side.
shortTitle: Container With Most Water: Opposite-End, Move the Shorter Side
keyPoints: Water is limited by the shorter wall, so moving the shorter pointer inward is the only move that can possibly increase the area.
Area = min(h[left], h[right]) * (right - left); O(n) time, O(1) space.
Correctness: discarding the shorter line never loses a better answer because all remaining pairs with that line have less width.
Equal heights: moving either pointer is correct since both are identically limited.
The brute-force all-pairs approach is O(n squared) and unnecessary.
This is the canonical example of the greedy opposite-end two-pointer pattern.

s1_definition.oneliner: Water is limited by the shorter wall, so moving the shorter pointer inward is the only move that can possibly increase the area.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Container With Most Water** – find two vertical lines from an array of heights that form the container holding the most water.
- **Area** – `min(h[left], h[right]) * (right - left)`; limited by the shorter wall.
- **Greedy rule** – always move the pointer at the shorter line inward; moving the taller line cannot improve the area.
- **Correctness** – discarding the shorter line is safe because all remaining pairs using it have less width and at most the same height.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of each bar as the balance on a day, and we want the widest, deepest reserve pool we can form between two days. The water level is capped by the shorter of the two day-balances, and the width is the number of days between them. Rajesh starts with the first and last day, keeps whichever is taller, and moves the shorter day inward hoping to find a taller wall that holds more.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  balances = [3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 2, 6]
              L                    R

  Step 1: L=0(3), R=6(6)  area = 3*6 = 18
          3 < 6 --> move L
  Step 2: L=1(1), R=6(6)  area = 1*5 = 5
          1 < 6 --> move L
  Step 3: L=2(2), R=6(6)  area = 2*4 = 8
          2 < 6 --> move L
  Step 4: L=3(4), R=6(6)  area = 4*3 = 12
          4 < 6 --> move L
  Step 5: L=4(5), R=6(6)  area = 5*2 = 10
          5 < 6 --> move L
  Step 6: L=5(2), R=6(6)  area = 2*1 = 2
          2 < 6 --> move L
  L >= R --> stop

  Best area = 18 (lines at index 0 and 6)

  Correctness:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ shorter wall --> limited height       │
  │ moving shorter: only chance to gain   │
  │ moving taller:  can only lose or stay │
  │ discarding shorter: all remaining     │
  │   pairs with it have less width       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Container With Most Water asks me to pick two vertical lines from an array of heights so the container they form holds the most water. I solve it with opposite-end two pointers starting at the first and last lines. At each step I compute the area (shorter height times width), update my running maximum, and move the pointer at the shorter line inward.

The reason I always move the shorter side is the heart of the solution. The area is capped by the shorter line, so moving the taller line inward would only shrink the width while the height stays limited, and the area could never improve. Moving the shorter line is the only move that gives a chance at a taller limiting wall. When both heights are equal, moving either side is fine because both are identically limited.

The subtle guarantee is that discarding the shorter line never loses a better answer, because any other pair that used that short line as its limit would have had less width and at most the same height, so it could not beat the area I already recorded. That is why the greedy pass is correct.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this for the treasury dashboard to find the liquidity window between two days with the largest sustained reserve. With thousands of days, an all-pairs scan was too slow for an interactive dashboard, and the linear two-pointer approach made it responsive.

Remember one sentence: opposite-end pointers, always move the shorter wall inward, and discarding it is safe because all remaining pairs with it have less width and cannot beat the recorded area.
